Lessons.Title: Represent Arrays with Expressions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: represent equal-group array situations using physical objects or drawings and multiplication expressions; reverse the work by drawing rows and columns for given expressions. These are independently authored explanations aligned to the published 2021 first-edition source. No publisher artwork is reused.

Warm-up, How Many Do You See (10 minutes): the original image contains five rows of four triangles, 20 triangles altogether. Students use subitizing or grouped counting, then discuss where they see groups. This is more than the numerical question 5×4=20; the teacher checks visual grouping strategies. The original triangle artwork needs separate image-rights review.

Activity 1, Represent Array Situations (20 minutes): provide 20 connecting cubes or counters for each pair and ask students to represent four source contexts as arrays BEFORE writing multiplication expressions. Situation 1: 3 rows of 5 chairs, 3×5 or 5×3. Situation 2: 4 rows of 5 cars, 4×5 or 5×4. Situation 3: 2 rows of 6 eggs, 2×6 or 6×2. Situation 4: 2 lines of 10 students, 2×10 or 10×2. Either orientation can be justified by reading rows or columns, but the source array drawing is always teacher-reviewed. MLR2 Collect and Display reinforces row, column, each, 3 by 5, and corresponding expressions. Offer counter models for students who need perceptual support.

Activity 2, Connect Arrays to Expressions (15 minutes): start by forming a HUMAN array for 4×6 with the whole class (adjust when the class size is different). Then students draw three independent rectangular arrays representing 2×3, 5×2 and 4×4. They discuss which factor maps to a row or column and how equal groups remain visible. Drawn accuracy and partner reasoning cannot be auto-graded from the product alone.

Synthesis (10 minutes): have children compare a story, its array of objects or drawn rows and columns, and the associated multiplication expression; explain group count, objects in each group and total. A 5-minute original publisher Cool-down titled Array Situation is access-restricted: Edulytics supplies a separate first-party task asking for a sketch, expression and justification and does not claim to reproduce the original.

2021 original source-verified media: publisher warm-up shows five rows of four small triangles (20 shapes). The original triangle SVG's twenty individual triangular paths were inspected. Edulytics's own independently drawn CSS geometry preserves five complete rows, four shapes each, without reusing the publisher vector artwork or logo.

2021 official Student Task Statements PDF: three pages. Page 1 asks about a five-by-four triangle picture. Page 2 lists all four original contexts, explicitly requiring an array drawing for EACH and a multiplication expression for EACH. Page 3 requires three independent rectangular arrays for 2×3, 5×2, 4×4, plus reasoning. The human 4×6 class array appears in original teacher guidance, not as a uniquely graded digital product.

2021 teacher lesson explicitly permits reversed factor order with corresponding array interpretation, while emphasizing original students have not yet formally learned commutativity. MLR2 Collect and Display supports row, column, each, for every and the multiple expressions; Representation supports gesturing/drawing while explaining factor roles. Teacher may use bodies for a 4×6 array, adapting to actual class size and having extra learners observe/reason. Teacher reflection collects observations to use in the later source commutativity lesson. Optional centers: Capture Squares Stage 5 and Five in a Row: Multiplication Stage 1.

All original nine learnable A1/A2 array/representation subtasks are addressed separately: four written-expression fields with parallel human-judged four drawings, whole-class 4×6 body construction and three independent student diagrams. The source-specific first-party Rich V2 is materialized through existing source-edition/canonical-body-hash guarded correction code. This is academic authoring only: original screenshots, answers from student submissions, and test/CI/Stage D runtime are not claimed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplication expressions from arrays
KeyConcepts.Definition: An expression identifies how rows and columns group a total.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write the pair of factors; the source accepts either justified orientation when the array can be read by rows or columns.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 rows of 5 chairs may be represented by 3×5 or 5×3 with a clear group explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Arrays must be constructed
KeyConcepts.Definition: An array is a complete equal-row, equal-column layout.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The object or sketch must use all objects with consistent rows and columns; a correct number is not enough.
KeyConcepts.Example: 2 rows of 6 eggs represent twelve eggs; 2×6 is only its expression.

KeyConcepts.Title: Row-column flexibility
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rectangular array can be interpreted by equal rows or equal columns.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Reversed factors may represent the same pictured layout without changing the total.
KeyConcepts.Example: 4×5 and 5×4 can both describe twenty arranged objects.

KeyConcepts.Title: Counter models and accessibility
KeyConcepts.Definition: Physical cubes or counters provide a manipulable array representation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Teachers give each pair twenty and permit multiple strategies, using source MLR2 vocabulary support.
KeyConcepts.Example: Students move twenty counters into four rows of five to illustrate a story.

WorkedExamples.Title: Triangle visual groups
WorkedExamples.Question: An original illustration shows five equal rows of four triangles.
WorkedExamples.Method: Group visible shapes and add five equal rows.
Steps: Count four triangles in each row.
Multiply five by four to get twenty.
Explain which visible group structure supported the count.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher assesses the grouping observation against source visual.

WorkedExamples.Title: Chairs in three rows
WorkedExamples.Question: Three rows contain five chairs each. Draw the array and write an expression.
Steps: Arrange 15 counters in three equally filled rows.
Write 3×5, or 5×3 if explaining the column interpretation.
Give a teacher the array sketch and rationale.
WorkedExamples.Check: Expression accepts either order; drawing and group explanation need human assessment.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cars, eggs and student lines
WorkedExamples.Question: Represent 4 rows of 5 cars, 2 rows of 6 eggs, and 2 lines of 10 students.
WorkedExamples.Method: Build or draw each as a separate complete rectangle.
Steps: Cars: four equal rows of five, expression 4×5 or 5×4.
Eggs: two rows of six, 2×6 or 6×2.
Students: two lines of ten, 2×10 or 10×2.
Justify each factor using physical rows or columns.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 20 cars, 12 eggs, 20 students with matching expression pairs.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source requires both diagram and expression.

WorkedExamples.Title: Draw arrays from supplied expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw separate arrays for 2×3, 5×2 and 4×4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use one factor to count complete rows and the other for equal items per row.
Steps: Draw two full rows of three.
Draw five full rows of two.
Draw four full rows of four.
Explain how the matching columns provide an alternate equal-group view.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 6, 10, and 16 objects in three correct rectangular drawings.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews each picture; numerical totals alone do not pass.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Entering only the total such as 20 for a requested multiplication expression.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A total does not identify either multiplication factor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write both factors in the expression and separately draw the source array.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original teacher synthesis permits students to read equal groups across rows or columns.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept 3×5 or 5×3, and have the teacher confirm the diagram explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using four circles of five instead of a complete row/column array.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The activity explicitly requires an array arrangement, not merely equal groups.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align each row and check that columns are complete.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the class human array as a uniquely numeric exercise.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The objective is physically forming and explaining a 4×6 model adapted to attendance.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require teacher review of the actual physical or drawn construction.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up: 5 rows of 4 triangles, total 20, with visual reasoning.
Activity 1: 4 source contexts with 3×5, 4×5, 2×6 and 2×10 factor pairs and FOUR array drawings.
Any factor orientation supported by source row/column mapping is admissible; written expression is separate from human-graded drawing.
Activity 2: classroom 4×6 body array (attendance-adaptable), then 2×3, 5×2 and 4×4 drawings.
Teacher preparation requires 20 counters/cubes per pair and MLR2 learner language support.
Published source Cool-down is gated; independent first-party drawing task is not publisher reproduction.

The original 2021 5×4 triangle source SVG and 3-page Student Task Statements PDF were source-reviewed and independently modeled; runtime materialization and classroom student work remain unrun/unassessed.
No tests/CI/Stage D/academic sign-off/merge/deployment have occurred.
2021 accessibility uses MLR2 Collect and Display plus Representation with gestures/drawings. Teacher reflection anticipates future commutativity.
